To go deeper here, because I suspect you mean chemicals can be found in clothing that may cause you to have an immune response (or worse) to them. First step when you bring washable garments home would be to run them through the laundry. That should take care of most anything you could have a reaction from. "Dry Clean Only" garments tend to be only those things made from natural or animal materials that change their dimensions when water is involved in their care. Some things have bits of cardboard or other water-softened bits in them, so dry cleaning is prescribed for them.

Most clothing are treated with dyes and then fixing agents to stabilize the dyes. A water wash at the end of the manufacturing process represents additional cost to the maker, and also degrades the marketability because that first wash can dull the color of a garment. There may be some dye left over that hasn't bonded to the fabric. Textile dyes are chosen for their color, first and foremost. Their toxicity is a secondary thing, but much of that can be abated through fixing agents or ensuring that the dye is fast to the fabric (won't rub off or leech out with water or sweat). Some are only acid-reactive. Your sweat contains salt, oils, and skin cells that when degraded can lower the pH from neutral. The eventual discoloration is the result of dyes reacting to acids from this and may exhibit another color.

The industrial use of dyes has a checkered history, with some being rather toxic like when the preferred dye for red being an amalgam of mercury, while others may have come from the family of organophosphates --the same group of chemicals best known for being used as pesticides and neurochemical agents for wartime use. Natural dyes are kindof a nitchy consumer market.
